datatype.name: SyllogisticFigure
datatype.definition: The figure of a categorical syllogism (1-4): the schematic arrangement of the middle term across the two premises.

provenance.ref: Book I, chs. 4-6 (the first three figures)
provenance.note: Aristotle sets out three figures; the fourth is a later, post-Aristotelian addition, so the bound admits 1-4.

enumeration.name: CategoricalForm
enumeration.definition: The four standard forms of a categorical proposition, classified by quantity (universal/particular) and quality (affirmative/negative).

provenance.ref: Book I.1 (premises as universal/particular and affirmative/negative)
provenance.note: The A/E/I/O letter mnemonic is the later, medieval naming of these four forms.

value.definition: 'Some S are not P' (traditionally labelled O).

interface.name: ITruthBearer
interface.definition: The contract of a truth-bearer: anything that can be true or false and so can stand as a premise or a conclusion. Classical bivalence is assumed here; non-classical logics that admit further or indeterminate values are a known and legitimate departure.

provenance.note: A behaviour contract over the philosophical notion of a truth-bearer; no bivalence claim is asserted about the world.

concept.name: PhilosophicalConcept
concept.definition: An abstract idea or universal that is an object of philosophical analysis (e.g. justice, causation, identity, being).

provenance.note: An L0 category-C abstract entity and the root of the philosophy.concepts sub-domain, left as an extension point for specific concepts. WMOOP records such concepts' structure without asserting their metaphysical status; realism vs. nominalism about abstracta is itself contested.

concept.name: Proposition
concept.definition: A truth-apt content that is either true or false and can be affirmed, denied, or offered as a premise or a conclusion.

provenance.note: Modelled as the primary bearer of truth-value. Whether propositions exist as mind-independent abstracta is contested; WMOOP commits only to their structural role.

property.name: content
property.definition: A representative natural-language statement of the proposition. The proposition itself is language-neutral; this string is only one expression of it.

concept.name: CategoricalProposition
concept.definition: A proposition that affirms or denies a predicate of a subject in one of the four standard forms, as used in categorical syllogisms.

property.name: form
property.definition: Which of the four standard categorical forms the proposition has.

concept.name: Argument
concept.definition: A structured set of propositions in which one or more premises are offered in support of a conclusion.

provenance.note: Structural characterisation (premises support a conclusion), neutral between deductive and inductive support.

property.name: premiseCount
property.definition: The number of premises the argument offers (the arity of its hasPremise relation), exposed as a constrainable scalar.

invariant.message: An argument must offer at least one premise.

relation.name: hasPremise
relation.definition: A proposition offered in support of the conclusion.

relation.name: hasConclusion
relation.definition: The proposition the premises are offered to support.

concept.name: DeductiveArgument
concept.definition: An argument whose conclusion is claimed to follow of necessity from its premises, so that it is valid or invalid.

property.name: valid
property.definition: Whether the argument is formally valid - its conclusion follows of necessity from its premises. A property to be assessed per argument, not asserted here.

concept.name: InductiveArgument
concept.definition: An argument whose premises are offered to make the conclusion probable rather than necessary, so that it is strong or weak rather than valid.

provenance.note: The modern deductive/inductive contrast turns on necessary vs. merely probable support.

property.name: strong
property.definition: Whether the premises lend the conclusion strong, as opposed to weak, support. Inductive strength is a matter of degree; this records the coarse assessment.

concept.name: Syllogism
concept.definition: A categorical syllogism: a deductive argument with exactly two categorical premises and a categorical conclusion, linked through a shared middle term.

provenance.ref: Book I, chs. 1-7 (the categorical syllogism and its figures)

property.name: figure
property.definition: The figure (1-4) fixing the position of the middle term across the premises.

concept.name: PhilosophicalPosition
concept.definition: A stance on a philosophical question, characterised by the propositions it affirms as true (for example a thesis such as realism or dualism).

provenance.note: An extension point for specific positions. WMOOP records which theses a position affirms WITHOUT asserting that the position is correct.

relation.name: assertsThesis
relation.definition: A proposition the position holds to be true.

relation.name: addressesBranch
relation.definition: The branch of philosophy the position belongs to.

concept.name: AristotelianCategory
concept.definition: One of the ten highest kinds (categories) under which, in Aristotle's scheme, anything that can be said of a subject falls.

provenance.note: Modelled as ONE named, sourced category scheme, NOT the unique partition of being; rival schemes exist (e.g. Kant's twelve categories). `kind: concrete` so the ten categories are L2 individuals - an abstract entity enumerated by its members, as wmoop.education/CurriculumSubject is.

property.name: greekTerm
property.definition: The transliterated Greek term Aristotle uses for the category.

concept.name: Branch
concept.definition: A major field of philosophical inquiry, distinguished by the kind of question it asks.

provenance.note: The partition of philosophy into branches is a CONVENTION, not a unique or empirical division: logic is also claimed by mathematics, and ethics and aesthetics are sometimes grouped together as axiology. `kind: concrete` so the branches are L2 individuals.

property.name: centralQuestion
property.definition: A short statement of the central question the branch addresses.

individual.name: Substance
individual.definition: What a thing is - the category of independent beings (Aristotle's examples: man, horse).

individual.name: Quantity
individual.definition: How much or how many something is (Aristotle's examples: four-foot, five-foot).

individual.name: Quality
individual.definition: What sort of thing something is (Aristotle's examples: white, grammatical).

individual.name: Relation
individual.definition: How something stands to something else (Aristotle's examples: double, half, greater).

individual.name: Place
individual.definition: Where something is (Aristotle's examples: in the Lyceum, in the market-place).

individual.name: Time
individual.definition: When something is (Aristotle's examples: yesterday, last year). The category of 'when', distinct from the physical quantity of time.

individual.name: Position
individual.definition: The posture in which something is placed (Aristotle's examples: is lying, is sitting).

individual.name: State
individual.definition: The condition of having something (Aristotle's examples: has shoes on, has armour on).

individual.name: Action
individual.definition: The doing of something (Aristotle's examples: to cut, to burn).

individual.name: Affection
individual.definition: The undergoing of something, being acted upon (Aristotle's examples: to be cut, to be burned).

individual.name: Metaphysics
individual.definition: The study of what there is and the fundamental nature of reality: being, objects, properties, causation, time and possibility.
individual.value: What is there, and what is its fundamental nature?

individual.name: Epistemology
individual.definition: The study of knowledge: its nature, sources, limits and justification, and the difference between knowledge and mere belief.
individual.value: What is knowledge, and what can we know?

individual.name: Ethics
individual.definition: The study of right action, the good, and how one ought to live.
individual.value: What ought one to do, and what is a good life?

provenance.ref: Book I (the good and the end of action)
provenance.note: One foundational treatment; the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy also covers normative, meta- and applied ethics.

individual.name: Logic
individual.definition: The study of valid inference and the forms of correct reasoning. Its status as a branch of philosophy, rather than of mathematics, is itself debated.
individual.value: What distinguishes a valid inference from an invalid one?

provenance.note: Aristotle's founding of formal logic; the field now extends far beyond the syllogistic.

individual.name: Aesthetics
individual.definition: The study of beauty, taste and the nature and value of art and aesthetic experience.
individual.value: What is beauty, and what is the nature of art?
